idiom_name: struct with private state (or final class when reference semantics are required)
implementation_notes: Swift's default answer to 'what kind of type is this?' is the value type: a struct has value semantics, its members can be `private` or `private(set)`, and `internal` (the default access level) already hides the type outside its module unless it is explicitly marked `public`, with `fileprivate` narrowing to one file - which replaces the classic 'class with private members' structure while keeping the type's definition in one place. The Swift book recommends preferring structs and using classes only for reference semantics, identity or Objective-C interop, in which case `final` (or a `final` class) prevents a subclass from attaching meaning the class does not state; an `enum` with associated values is the third standalone form, adding a closed set of cases and no external concepts.
pitfalls: Value equality is not automatic: without `Equatable`/`Hashable` conformance two instances are never `==`, and synthesis compares stored properties only, so reference-typed members compare by identity.
A struct holding a reference type is only shallowly immutable: the referenced object can still mutate behind the value, so keep members value-typed or copy on the way in.
Classes are subclassable inside the module and `open` across modules; a type whose semantics matter should be `final` (or a struct) so another file cannot re-attach meaning.
Protocol conformances placed in other files split the type's definition across the module - exactly the fragmentation this pattern avoids - so keep them with the type.
